evidence: src/application/use-cases/StartSubscription.ts execute(): `if (!Number.isInteger(seats) || seats < 1) { throw new SubscriptionError('invalid', 'A subscription needs at least one whole seat'); }` is a rule every subscription must follow, so it belongs in the domain layer
execute() then calls `Subscription.start(this.subscriptions.nextId(), customerId, plan, seats)`, the domain entry point that should enforce the seat rule itself
The rest of execute() is proper application work: plans.find, subscriptions.activeFor, subscriptions.save and summarise(), all through ports or DTOs
parsedVerdict.reasoning: Most of StartSubscription.execute is proper application work: it looks up the plan through the PlanCatalog port, checks for a duplicate through the SubscriptionRepository port, builds the subscription with Subscription.start, saves it and returns a DTO. One rule doesn't belong there. The seat check (seats must be a whole number of at least 1, with the message 'A subscription needs at least one whole seat') is a rule every subscription must follow, so it belongs in the domain layer. Subscription.start already takes seats, so the domain model should be the one rejecting a bad value. Keeping the check in the use case either duplicates the rule or means the domain model can create an invalid subscription when called from anywhere else. The one-subscription-per-plan check is acceptable in the application layer because it needs a repository lookup across several subscriptions. Confidence is moderate because some teams treat a seat check like this as ordinary input validation, which is fine in the application layer.
